archetype.name: Rebuilding (young-QB growth year)
archetype.definition: A team built around Cam Ward's development. The record is bad and mostly earned, and the season is judged by whether the offense becomes real before the roster around it does.

report.headline: Ward's offense woke up in late October; the pass defense started leaking instead.
report.take:
This is still a rebuilding team, and the dossier doesn't hide it. The Titans are 1-7, last in the AFC South, 31st in offensive EPA, 32nd in yards per game and 32nd in time of possession. Cam Ward has started every game, so there is no quarterback split to blame. What the first two months showed is that the offense couldn't stay on the field and the defense had to absorb too many possessions. It follows two 3-win, 14-loss seasons, so the losing isn't new. It is slightly less bad: net EPA has improved from -0.252 last year to -0.166, and the defense has climbed from 28th to 23rd in EPA allowed.

The early record was built on a broken passing game. Through the first five weeks Ward's passing EPA was negative almost every week. It bottomed out in a 3-26 home loss to Houston with -16.9 passing EPA, four sacks and 83 penalty yards. The Week 6 win at Indianapolis came from the defense, with six sacks and three takeaways, while the offense threw for 102 yards. Then things flipped. Passing EPA was +5.9 against Cleveland and +8.7 at Cincinnati, where Tennessee scored 36 points and ran for 158 yards. The protection numbers support the idea that it can last: 4th in QB hit rate allowed and 9th in sack rate.

The 1-7 hides that this team keeps games close and then loses them. The Titans have a 20% one-score win rate and sit at -1.4 wins over expected, and the point differential implies 2.4 wins. They have covered four times as an underdog, including 11.5 at Baltimore and 13.5 at Cincinnati. Robert Saleh's group is disciplined (4th-fewest penalties) and the most aggressive fourth-down team in the league. It is also a sure-tackling defense, 2nd in missed-tackle rate. The flaw is the pass defense:
- 27th in pass EPA allowed
- 30th against short passes
- 29th in explosive pass rate
- 308 passing yards allowed to Cleveland and 462 to Cincinnati in the last two games

The offense got better just as the pass defense got worse, and that is why they lost both of those games.

From here, expect a few more wins than the first half produced, but not a turnaround. The close-game luck should even out somewhat. The bad news is that the efficiency profile still belongs to a bottom-five team, and the next game is against one of the AFC's best.

strengths.title: Protection keeps Ward upright
strengths.body: Pressure gets home at an average rate, but Ward rarely takes hits: 4th in QB hit rate allowed and 9th in sack rate. The run game also avoids negative plays, 6th in stuff rate. The line is doing its job, so the offense's problems sit downstream of it. That holds only while Skoronski and Latham, both 90%+ snap starters, stay healthy.

strengths.title: The passing game turned a corner
strengths.body: After five weeks of negative passing EPA, including -16.9 against Houston, Ward posted +5.9 against Cleveland and +8.7 at Cincinnati. Two games is a small sample, and Cincinnati's defense is mid-pack. Still, the improvement shows up in both yardage and scoring. Losing Carnell Tate, the target leader, tests whether it was Ward or the matchups.

strengths.title: Disciplined, aggressive, sure-tackling
strengths.body: Saleh's team plays clean, with the 4th-fewest penalties per game. It tackles well, 2nd in missed-tackle rate, and it goes for it on fourth down more than anyone. That is a well-coached floor that keeps the Titans within a score of better teams. It doesn't create wins on its own, but it lasts, because it comes from coaching choices rather than luck.

concerns.title: Offense can't hold the ball
concerns.body: The Titans are 31st in offensive EPA, 32nd in yards per game and 32nd in time of possession. The defense faces too many snaps, and the yards-allowed ranking is worse than the per-play numbers would suggest. This is the core problem of the season. The last two games are the first evidence it can change.

concerns.title: Pass defense bleeds underneath and explosive
concerns.body: Against the run the defense is respectable. Against the pass it is 30th on short throws and 29th in explosive pass rate. Cincinnati threw for 462 yards on it. Opponents have mostly run against this defense in neutral situations, which suggests teams haven't yet needed to attack it through the air. Good passing offenses will.

concerns.title: Close losses, some of it luck
concerns.body: The record understates the team a little. It has a 20% one-score win rate and is 1.4 wins under expectation. Some of that should regress toward normal. But the point differential still implies only 2.4 wins, so better luck turns this into a 4- or 5-win team, not a contender.

trend.note: The offense bottomed out against Houston in Week 5 and has climbed since, putting up its best passing games in Weeks 7 and 8. Over the same two games the pass defense got worse, so the results haven't followed.

nextGame.headline: Rested Titans host a Jaguars team missing both safeties
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville comes in 5-2 and leading the division. It is 4th in net EPA and 2nd in point differential per game, and it has a top-five passing offense. Its defense is elite against the run (2nd in rush EPA) and against short throws (1st). It is 29th in EPA allowed on deep passes. Opponents throw on the Jaguars more than almost anyone, which fits a defense that shuts off the run. That is a bad fit for a Titans offense that runs more than expected. Tennessee is coming off the bye with 14 days of rest at home. There is no line in the dossier yet.

Availability could swing it. Jacksonville has lost safeties Antonio Johnson (out) and Eric Murray (out for the season) and DT DaVon Hamilton (season). Travon Walker, Jakobi Meyers and back Bhayshul Tuten are questionable, with return estimates ahead of this game. For Tennessee, WR Carnell Tate (the target leader) and RB Tyjae Spears are listed out. Starting linemen Peter Skoronski and JC Latham are questionable, and so is CB Marcus Harris. Their return estimates land on game day, so treat them as hopeful rather than certain. Punter Tommy Townsend is also out.

waysToWin.title: Throw deep at the depleted secondary
waysToWin.body: Jacksonville's defense chokes off short passes but is 29th on deep throws, and it is now without both starting-caliber safeties. With the bye to prepare and Ward coming off his two best passing games, Tennessee's best path is vertical shots off play-action, not grinding underneath. WR3s have scored more against Jacksonville than against any other defense, so Elic Ayomanor in a bigger role is a real lever.

waysToWin.title: Keep it close and play clean
waysToWin.body: Tennessee is one of the least-penalized teams, and Jacksonville ranks 21st in penalties per game. The Titans' fourth-down aggression and sure tackling have kept them within a score of better teams all year. If they avoid giving away field position, a late one-score game at home gives their luck a chance to turn.

waysToLose.title: Lawrence picks apart the soft middle
waysToLose.body: Jacksonville's pass offense ranks 5th in EPA, and Tennessee's pass defense is 30th against short throws and 29th on explosives. The last two opponents threw for 300-plus. Jacksonville can move the ball efficiently and avoid the run defense entirely, and it is unclear if CB Marcus Harris plays.

waysToLose.title: The run-first plan hits a wall
waysToLose.body: Tennessee leans toward the run, and Jacksonville is 2nd in rush EPA allowed and one of the strongest pass funnels in the league. Without Spears, and with Pollard carrying the load, early-down runs likely set up long third downs. That points to the stalled, low-possession games of September.

waysToLose.title: Line injuries and giveaways
waysToLose.body: If Skoronski or Latham can't go, Tennessee's best unit loses a starter. The offense has already turned it over 12 times, against a Jacksonville team that ranks 5th in turnover margin. Short fields for the Jaguars would end this early.

nextGame.watch: Whether Tennessee actually takes deep shots at a Jacksonville secondary missing both safeties, or plays into the Jaguars' run defense the way its season tendencies suggest.

restOfSeason.body:
The second half has more openings than the first. Dallas (32nd in defensive EPA) and Detroit (30th) have porous defenses, and Washington, Indianapolis, Houston and Las Vegas are middling or worse. Two dates with Jacksonville and one with Pittsburgh are the clear tough games. An improving Ward and some regression in close games should produce a few more wins. Expect three to five, not a push for relevance.

The protection and the discipline should hold. The late-October passing surge is real enough to build on, but the opponents behind it were average. The 36-point output in Cincinnati isn't a new baseline. The pass defense is the part most likely to keep costing games, because offenses are now attacking it through the air. Tate's return and the health of the two starting linemen set the offense's ceiling.
swingFactors: Whether Ward's Weeks 7-8 passing holds up against good defenses
Carnell Tate's and the starting linemen's returns
Pass defense vs. the short and explosive passing game

confidence.note: Eight games with one quarterback make the profile clear, but the offensive turn rests on two games and the injury report is in flux.
